The pt2399-core board AS THE AGENT TOOLING PRODUCED IT, placed and unrouted:
the bytes committed by f3b295b, "pcb: stop the hole placer deleting real parts,
and make its output idempotent", which is the last commit that wrote this board
while it was still an agent artifact. Not re-authored.

THAT CLAIM IS PINNED IN CODE, NOT HERE. tests/pcb/placed-board-fixture.test.ts
holds the file's sha256 and fails if these bytes change, because a provenance
claim in prose is a transcription with a date on it. This file says where the
bytes came from; that one is what keeps the statement true.

WHY A COPY EXISTS AT ALL, and it is a different reason from the empty fixture's
next door. On 2026-11-17 the owner looked at the two candidates the Phase 1
probe routed, said both were acceptable but that "some of the layout choices are
a little odd", and asked to start from one and make manual edits in KiCad.
circuits/pt2399-core/pt2399-core.kicad_pcb is therefore HIS file from that point
on, hand-edited, and no longer the output of any tool here.

Eight tests had been reading it as though it were. They broke the moment the
routed candidate was adopted, in two groups, and both were reading the live
board for a property only the agent-produced board has:

  - tests/pcb/mounting-hole-placement.test.ts asserted that running the
    mounting-hole placer on the committed board reproduces it BYTE FOR BYTE, and
    that its origins carry the board's own six-decimal spelling. The routing
    engine rewrote both - it expanded the keepout Rule Areas into explicit
    vertex lists and re-spelled 14.000000 as 14 - so the assertions failed on
    formatting, not on geometry.

  - the five pour-refill configuration tests and one pour-refill test build a
    fixture by COPYING the real board and adding one full-board ground zone,
    with "the real board is only COPIED, into scratch; it has no pour and is not
    changed" written in the file. The adopted board brought the router's own
    ground zone with it, so each fixture ended up with two ground zones on B.Cu
    declaring different thermal gaps, and readGroundPour refused them - which is
    that guard working correctly on a board the test did not expect.

KICAD WOULD HAVE BROKEN THEM AGAIN ANYWAY, which is the argument for a fixture
rather than for re-baselining the numbers. Both groups rest on byte-level and
zone-level properties of a file a person is now going to open and save, and
KiCad rewrites formatting throughout on every save. Re-pinning them against the
adopted board would buy one green run and go red on the owner's first edit.

WHAT IS AND IS NOT CHECKED AGAINST THE LIVE BOARD AFTER THIS. Checks of the
DELIVERABLE still read the owner's board and are meant to: schematic parity, DRC
(including his 2 mm courtyard rule), the floorplan grade, and the silkscreen
widths. Those SHOULD fail if a hand edit breaks a fab rule or his own spacing
rule - that is the safety net he asked for. What moved here is only the tests of
the TOOLING, whose subject is what the tool produces.

This is not a reduced or synthetic board. It is the real 150 x 100 mm board with
all 28 footprints at the settled positions, the four M3 holes and their keepout
Rule Areas, no tracks and no pour.
